notes:
I've gathered substantial material from Enduring Word (David Guzik), Ellicott, Pulpit Commentary, Gill's Exposition, and several other sources. Let me compile the verse-by-verse notes.

---

## Deuteronomy 21 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview
The chapter contains five laws united by the theme of the sacredness of human life and personal rights (Pulpit Commentary). Kline notes these can also be grouped as limits on the authority of the head of the household: regarding a captive wife, a preferred wife's son, and a rebellious son (Coffman, citing Kline).  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-21.html  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/deuteronomy-21.html

---

### vv. 1–9: Atonement for an Unsolved Murder

**v. 1 — "If one is found slain…and it is not known who killed him"**
- Presumes death from natural causes has been ruled out; this is a clear murder case with an unknown perpetrator (Guzik, Enduring Word). Gill adds that the body must be found "in the field" — not under a heap, not hanging on a tree, and not swimming on water (citing the Mishnah, Sotah 9:2).  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-21/  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-21.html

- The theological concern is that unavenged blood defiles and pollutes the land (Numbers 35:33–34). Therefore, even an unsolved murder required cleansing (Guzik). Pulpit Commentary says the whole land would be involved in the guilt unless duly expiated.  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-21/  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-21.html

**v. 2 — "Your elders and judges must come out and measure the distance"**
- Rashi says these were special commissioners from the great Sanhedrin in Jerusalem. Gill notes the Mishnah specifies three go out from the great Sanhedrin (R. Judah says five). They measure from the body to surrounding cities to determine jurisdiction — the nearest city bears responsibility for expiation.  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-21.html  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-21.html

- Ellicott comments that even in modern times, the most effectual remedy against undiscovered outrages is a fine upon the district where they occur.  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-21.html

**v. 3 — "A heifer that has never been yoked or used for work"**
- The heifer was to be a yearling, not two years old (Gill, citing Jewish writers). It had never been profaned by common use (Guzik, citing Thompson). Though expiatory, it was not a proper sacrifice — so it did not need to be "without blemish" as sacrificial animals did (Gill, citing Mishnah Sotah 9:5).  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-21.html  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-21/

**v. 4 — "A valley with running water that has not been plowed or sown, and break its neck there"**
- "Rough valley" is literally "a stream of perpetuity" — a perennial stream (Pulpit, correcting the KJV). The place was uncultivated, in a state of nature. Keil explains: the water of the brook-valley would suck in the blood and clean it away, and blood sucked in by the earth would not be brought to light again by ploughing (Pulpit citing Keil).  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-21.html

- Rashi's memorable note: "A yearling heifer which has borne no fruit shall come and be beheaded in a place which yields no fruit, to atone for the murder of the man whom they did not suffer to bear fruit" (Ellicott).  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-21.html

- **Important**: Breaking the heifer's neck was *not* a sacrificial act (no blood-shedding); it was a symbolic representation of inflicting death on the undiscovered murderer (Pulpit). Guzik notes it was a substitutionary atonement — the heifer suffered death in place of the unknown criminal (citing Kalland).  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-21/  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-21.html

- Gill typologically connects this to Christ: brought into a "rough valley" (this lower world), treated roughly, put to death at the instigation of elders, outside the gates at Golgotha (cf. Hebrews 13:11).  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-21.html

**v. 5 — "The priests, the sons of Levi, shall come forward"**
- The priests' presence gave the transaction sanction as valid. By their word (literally "upon their mouth") every controversy and every stroke was to be tried — they were the final judicial authority (Pulpit).  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-21.html

**v. 6 — "Wash their hands by the stream over the heifer"**
- This act indicated that the elders threw off from them, utterly repudiated, the charge of blood-guiltiness on behalf of their city (Pulpit). Guzik notes parallels with Psalm 26:6, 73:13, and warns that the gesture meant nothing if the elders had not truly done all they could — just as Pilate's hand-washing at Jesus' trial (Matthew 27:24) was an empty gesture.  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-21/  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-21.html

**v. 7 — "Our hands did not shed this blood, nor did our eyes see it"**
- Rashi explains: not that the magistrates are suspected, but they declare they have not contrived or procured the murder by any partnership in the deed (Ellicott). The Targum of Jonathan adds: "It is manifest before the Lord that he did not come into our hands, nor did we dismiss him" (Gill).  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-21.html  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-21.html

**v. 8 — "Accept this atonement, O LORD…do not hold the shedding of innocent blood against them"**
- "Be merciful" = "be propitiated" (literally, *cover*). The mercy seat is the "covering" of the Law protecting Israel from it (Ellicott). According to Rashi, this prayer is spoken by the *priests*, not the elders — and Ellicott finds this probable since no other part of the transaction is assigned to them.  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-21.html

- Guzik notes: though the word *kapar* ("atone") appears twice, this is not atonement within the sacrificial system (the heifer's blood was not offered); it is atonement for *justice* — the heifer died in place of the unknown criminal to clear the land (citing Kalland and Thompson).  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-21/

**v. 9 — "So you shall purge from among you the guilt of shedding innocent blood"**
- The Talmud (Sotah 9:7) clarifies: if afterwards the murderer were apprehended, he would still suffer the penalty (Pulpit). The Mishnah adds: if the murderer is found before the heifer is beheaded, the heifer goes free; if found after, it is buried in that place and the murderer is still slain (Gill).  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-21.html  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-21.html

---

### vv. 10–14: Marriage to a Captive Woman

**v. 10 — "When you go to war against your enemies…and you take them captive"**
- This refers to *voluntary* wars (not the commanded wars against the seven Canaanite nations or Amalek, where all were to be destroyed). The captives here are from nations outside Canaan (Pulpit, Gill, Guzik citing Merrill).  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-21.html  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-21.html

**v. 11 — "If you see a beautiful woman among them, and you desire her"**
- According to Jewish writers, the woman could be a virgin, wife, or widow — even another man's wife — because Gentile marriages were not recognised as valid by the Jews (Gill, citing Jarchi and Maimonides).  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-21.html

- Guzik stresses that God gave these commands precisely because the custom could be terribly abused; the law provides remarkable protections. The woman is not from the Canaanite nations (cf. Deuteronomy 7:3).  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-21/

**v. 12 — "Shave her head, trim her nails"**
- **Two competing interpretations among Jewish commentators**:
  1. These acts were to *spoil her beauty* so the man's passion might cool (Rashi, Jarchi, Aben Ezra, Ben Melech, Maimonides). The Targum of Onkelos renders "pare her nails" as "let her nails grow" — to make her appear ugly and disagreeable.
  2. These were signs of *purification* from former heathenism, preparatory to reception among the covenant people (Pulpit). Shaving the head was also a token of mourning for her lost parents and former life (Guzik, citing Clarke).  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-21.html  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-21.html  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-21.html

- Constable notes that these were rituals of purification customary in the ancient Near East (citing Keil and Delitzsch).  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-21.html (search result excerpt)

**v. 13 — "Put aside the clothing of her captivity…mourn her father and mother a full month"**
- The change of garments suggests a change of status (Guzik, citing Thompson). The mourning period implies a degree of willingness on the woman's part — "one can hardly conceive of all this taking place coercively" (Guzik, citing Merrill).  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-21/

- **Disputed point**: Some Jewish writers held that the Israelite soldier could lie with the captive woman *once* to gratify his lust before the rituals, but could not repeat it. However, others (R. Jochanan, Josephus, Philo, Abarbinel) insisted that the first congress was unlawful and marriage must wait until all conditions were fulfilled. Gill and Guzik affirm the latter view — the law gives no licence to violate the woman.  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-21.html

**v. 14 — "If you are not pleased with her, you are to let her go wherever she wishes…you must not sell her"**
- If the marriage was dissolved, the woman's social status was not impaired. She was not a slave to be sold, but was free (Guzik, citing Thompson). Ellicott notes this shows that, ordinarily, such captives would be sold as slaves — but Israel was restricted from doing so.  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-21/  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-21.html

- This starkly contrasts with common ancient Near Eastern practice and demonstrates God's regard for the dignity of captive women (Pulpit Homiletics).  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-21.html

---

### vv. 15–17: The Right of the Firstborn

**v. 15 — "If a man has two wives, one beloved and the other unloved"**
- "Hated" is idiomatic Hebrew for "preferred less" — not active hatred (Ellicott).  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-21.html

- **Important distinction**: Gray's Concise Commentary and Constable note that the Hebrew should be read "If a man *has had* two wives" — implying the first wife was dead at the time. The legislation does not approve polygamy; God tolerated it but never legalised it under Moses. Monogamy was God's original will (Genesis 2:24).  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jgc/deuteronomy-21.html  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-21.html

**v. 16 — "He must not appoint the son of the beloved wife as the firstborn"**
- The father is legally incapable of doing this (Pulpit: "is not able to make"). The law protects the son from a capricious father (Constable).  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-21.html

**v. 17 — "He must acknowledge the firstborn…by giving him a double portion"**
- "Double portion" = literally "a mouth of two" — i.e., a share equal to that of two others. If there were three sons, the estate would be divided into four parts, with the firstborn receiving two. Guzik notes this rule was notably *not* followed in the case of Solomon (citing Kalland).  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-21/  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-21.html

- The Pulpit Commentary notes that while the right of the firstborn to pre-eminence was recognised among all nations from earliest times, the assignment of a *double share* in the inheritance is a new and special provision, mentioned only here.  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-21.html

- Constable cites a scholarly debate: Gunkel and Noth argued "double" should be rendered "two-thirds," but Eryl Davies (VT 36:3, 1986) refutes this — it means twice as much as any other son.  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-21.html

---

### vv. 18–21: The Stubborn and Rebellious Son

**v. 18 — "If a man has a stubborn and rebellious son who does not obey…and does not listen when disciplined"**
- "Stubborn and rebellious" (*sôrêr û-môreh*) became proverbial in Hebrew as the worst form of reproach. The same words describe Israel's wickedness in Jeremiah 5:23 and the forefathers in Psalm 78:8 (Guzik, citing Kalland; Ellicott).  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-21/  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-21.html

- The son is past the age of accountability — not a small child or young teen, but one set in determined rebellion (Guzik). The parents must have done a good job raising him, calling him to obedience, and disciplining him appropriately (Guzik).  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-21/

**v. 19 — "His father and mother are to lay hold of him and bring him to the elders…to the gate"**
- The parents could *not* carry out the penalty themselves. They had to bring the son before impartial judges. This was a *control* of parental authority — contrasting sharply with Greek and Roman law, which gave fathers absolute power of life or death over children (Guzik; Pulpit).  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-21/  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-21.html

**v. 20 — "He is a glutton and a drunkard"**
- The Hebrew word translated "glutton" (*zôlēl*) includes more than excessive eating — it designates one who is prodigal, who squanders his means or his person by indulgence (Pulpit). "Glutton and drunkard" appears as a cliché for self-indulgence and lack of constructive activity (Guzik, citing Merrill). The same two words appear together in Proverbs 23:20–22, which seems a distinct reference to this law (Ellicott).  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-21.html  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-21.html

**v. 21 — "Then all the men of his city will stone him to death"**
- Stoning was the punishment for blasphemers and idolaters. The sin was not only against parents but against the whole community — rebellion against parents sowed seeds for cultural ruin (Guzik, citing Poole). Rashi says the Law cuts short the man's career, anticipating that when he has spent all his father's money, he will take to the road and become a public robber — better he die innocent of such crimes than guilty (Ellicott).  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-21/  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-21.html

- **Notable**: Poole says the Jews held that this law was *never actually put into practice* — it was made "for terror and prevention, and to render the authority of parents more sacred and powerful." We have no Scriptural example of it being carried out (Guzik).  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-21/

---

### vv. 22–23: The Body Hanged on a Tree

**v. 22 — "If a man has committed a sin worthy of death, and he is executed, and you hang his body on a tree"**
- **Crucial**: Hanging on a tree was *not* execution by strangulation. The person was first put to death (normally by stoning), and then the corpse was impaled or mounted on a tree or stake for public exposure as a deterrent (Guzik; Ellicott; Pulpit; Constable). Joshua 10:26–27 provides an example.  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-21/  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-21.html  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-21.html

**v. 23 — "You must not leave the body on the tree overnight…for anyone who is hung on a tree is under God's curse"**
- The corpse must be buried the same day. Even in the most severe judgment, mercy tempers justice — one day's exposure was deemed sufficient (Guzik, citing Clarke). Ellicott notes this was remarkably and providentially fulfilled in our Lord's death: the Jews, with an eye to this law, ensured Jesus was taken down and buried before sunset (John 19:31).  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-21/  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-21.html

- **Two interpretations of "accursed of God"** (Pulpit; Ellicott):
  1. Rashi: "He that is hanged is the curse (disgrace) of God" — i.e., an insult to God, since man is made in His image and thus given to public scorn. Rashi illustrates: "There were two twin brothers, one made king, the other hanged for robbery. Everyone who saw him said, 'There hangs the king!'"
  2. The more probable meaning: "a curse inflicted by God" — the transgressor is made to endure divine curse. This is the sense Paul picks up in Galatians 3:13.  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-21.html  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-21.html

- **The NT connection** (Paul in Galatians 3:13–14): Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law by *becoming a curse for us*. Jesus not only died in the place of His people but took their place as the accursed of God, hanged on a "tree" in open shame. He received the curse believers deserved, so they could receive the blessing of Abraham (Guzik).  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-21/

- G. Campbell Morgan: "The man was accursed of God because he was hanged on a tree. He was hanged on the tree because he was accursed of God. The hanging was the outward sign of the curse upon him" (Guzik).  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-21/

- **Reformed perspective** (Ligonier): The crucifixion on a tree demonstrates that Jesus bore the covenantal curse that Adam's rebellion brought upon mankind. John Calvin comments that Moses speaks "only of those malefactors who are unworthy of burial," and the hanged man is called "the curse of God" because this kind of punishment is detestable in itself. Yet the gospel is displayed: "The innocent and blessed Son of God was hung on a tree as though He was a reprehensible criminal, and He suffered…the covenantal curse—in our place."  
— https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/cursed-tree

- Ellicott provocatively adds: "We cannot see why he should be pronounced cursed, except for the sake of that which was designed by 'the determined counsel and foreknowledge of God,' that His Son Jesus Christ should bear our sins in His own body on the tree."  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-21.html

### Denominational Distinctives (Where Identifiable)

**Reformed / Presbyterian**  
- Ligonier (R.C. Sproul's ministry) ties vv. 22–23 firmly into covenant theology: the tree-cursing connects to Adam's fall at the Tree of Knowledge, and Christ's crucifixion on a tree satisfies the curse of the covenant of works. The Heidelberg Catechism Q&A 39 explicitly cites Deuteronomy 21:23 to show that Christ's death by crucifixion demonstrates He bore the curse we deserved.  
— https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/cursed-on-the-tree  
— https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/cursed-tree

**Baptist**  
- Gill (a Particular Baptist) provides extensive typological reading: the heifer points to Christ's expiatory death for secret/unknown sins; the rough valley to Christ's humiliation. He also emphasises the Jewish interpretive tradition (Mishnah, Targums, Rashi, Maimonides) in great detail.  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-21.html

**Methodist / Wesleyan**  
- Specific Methodist sources were not reached within search limits. The Pulpit Commentary (1880, broadly Anglican/Nonconformist) emphasises the homiletical themes of social justice: "the preciousness of one human life in the sight of God," and God's care for the individual against being "lost in the crowd." The Homiletics section treats the unsolved murder law as a precursor to modern coroners' inquests and an expression of the "solidarity of the race."  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-21.html

**Pentecostal / Charismatic**  
- David Guzik (Enduring Word, broadly charismatic evangelical) emphasises the substitutionary nature of the atonement throughout the chapter and the personal application that "believers no longer need to fear God's curse" because of Christ's work. His application is consistently Christocentric and devotional.  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-21/

**Catholic and Orthodox**  
- Not reached due to search limits.

**Modern Scholarship**  
- Not reached due to search limits.

**Debated Points Across Traditions**  
- **Polygamy**: Constable (Dallas Theological Seminary, dispensational) explicitly states that God did not approve of polygamy but tolerated it, legislating for life lived in disobedience to His will. Gray's Concise Commentary similarly reads v. 15 as "If a man *has had* two wives" (implying sequentially, not simultaneously).  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-21.html  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jgc/deuteronomy-21.html

- **The captive woman ritual**: Jewish interpreters are split on whether shaving the head and paring nails was meant to *repel* the man (make her ugly) or to *purify* her for incorporation into Israel. Gill reports both views; Pulpit and Guzik favour the purification/mourning interpretation.  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-21.html

- **Whether the rebellious son law was ever enforced**: Poole and Jewish tradition say it was never carried out — it served as a deterrent. No biblical example exists.  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-21/
